name: Utilitarianism
statement: The right action is the one that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number.
statementAccent: the greatest happiness for the greatest number
meaning: Utilitarianism is a consequentialist ethical theory holding that the morally right action is the one that maximizes overall utility, usually understood as happiness, well-being, or pleasure, for the greatest number of people. It is captured in the phrase the greatest happiness for the greatest number, and it treats everyone's happiness impartially, counting each person equally. The founder of classical utilitarianism was Jeremy Bentham, who held that human beings are governed by pleasure and pain and formulated the principle of utility, judging actions right insofar as they promote happiness and wrong insofar as they produce the reverse; he proposed a felicific, or hedonic, calculus for weighing pleasures and pains by dimensions such as intensity, duration, and certainty, and treated all pleasures as differing only in quantity. John Stuart Mill, in his 1861 work Utilitarianism, refined Bentham's view by distinguishing higher from lower pleasures, arguing that intellectual and moral pleasures are superior in kind to bodily ones, and writing that it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied, better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. Utilitarianism comes in varieties, including act utilitarianism, which judges each act by its consequences, and rule utilitarianism, which follows rules that maximize utility, and it has been hugely influential in ethics, economics, and public policy.
mechanism: Utilitarianism determines right action by evaluating the effects of actions on aggregate welfare. The principle of utility holds that an action is right to the extent that it tends to increase the total happiness, or reduce the total suffering, of all those affected, and wrong to the extent that it does the reverse; the right action among the alternatives is the one that produces the greatest net balance of good over bad. Crucially, the calculation is impartial: each person's happiness counts equally, so no one's welfare, including the agent's own, is given special weight. Bentham proposed to make this quantitative through the hedonic calculus, tallying pleasures and pains by their intensity, duration, certainty, nearness, fruitfulness, purity, and the number of people affected, treating pleasures as differing only in amount. Mill argued that pleasures also differ in quality, with the higher pleasures of intellect, imagination, and moral feeling counting for more than the lower pleasures of the body, so that a life rich in the higher pleasures is better even if less contented. The theory divides over the object of assessment: act utilitarianism applies the principle directly to each individual action, asking which act would maximize utility, while rule utilitarianism applies it to rules, holding that one should follow the rules whose general adoption would maximize utility, a move intended to accommodate justice and reliability. Later versions substitute preference-satisfaction or broader well-being for pleasure.

examples.text: Bentham proposed weighing pleasures and pains by intensity, duration, certainty, and other dimensions to compute the right action.
Mill argued intellectual and moral pleasures are superior in kind, writing it is better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.

variants.name: Act versus rule utilitarianism
variants.text: Applying the principle of utility directly to each act, versus following rules whose general adoption maximizes utility.

variants.name: Hedonistic versus preference utilitarianism
variants.text: Measuring utility as pleasure and the absence of pain, versus the satisfaction of preferences or broader well-being.

whyItMatters: Utilitarianism is one of the most influential ethical theories in history and the most famous form of consequentialism, offering a clear, impartial, and secular criterion for right and wrong based on maximizing well-being. Its central idea, that we should act so as to produce the greatest happiness for the greatest number, counting everyone's welfare equally, has shaped moral philosophy since Bentham and Mill and continues to frame debates in ethics. Beyond philosophy, utilitarian thinking underpins vast areas of practical decision-making: it is the intellectual basis of welfare economics and cost-benefit analysis, it informs public policy and the design of institutions, and it animates modern movements in animal welfare, associated with Peter Singer, and effective altruism. Its impartiality and its insistence that every person's happiness matters equally have progressive implications, historically supporting reforms in law, prisons, and the treatment of the marginalized. At the same time, utilitarianism has provoked some of the most important criticisms in ethics, concerning rights, justice, and the sacrifice of individuals, which have themselves advanced moral theory. As the theory that the right act maximizes overall happiness, utilitarianism is a cornerstone of modern ethical and policy thought.

identify the right action as the one producing the greatest net balance of good over bad for the greatest number.

limits: Utilitarianism faces powerful and much-discussed objections. Because it aims to maximize aggregate welfare, it can seem to justify sacrificing individuals or minorities for the greater good, violating rights and justice, as in cases where harming an innocent person would maximize total happiness. Robert Nozick's utility monster, a being that derives enormously more utility from resources than others lose, dramatizes how aggregation can demand feeding one at everyone's expense. John Rawls and others press the separateness of persons objection, that utilitarianism improperly treats society as if it were a single person and ignores that individuals are distinct, so that gains to some cannot simply cancel losses to others. The theory is also charged with being excessively demanding, with ignoring the fair distribution of welfare, and with facing the practical difficulty of measuring and comparing utility across people. So utilitarianism robustly holds that the right act maximizes overall happiness, understood as an influential theory facing serious objections about rights, justice, distribution, demandingness, and the separateness of persons.
misreadings: Utilitarianism is not the pursuit of one's own happiness; it is impartial, counting everyone's welfare equally, including strangers. It does not straightforwardly endorse sacrificing individuals whenever it seems to raise the total, since that very feature is its most criticized point and rule utilitarianism and other refinements try to accommodate justice. And it is not a settled truth, since objections about rights, distribution, and the separateness of persons are serious, so treating utilitarianism as selfish, as obviously licensing any sacrifice for the total, or as beyond challenge, misreads an influential but contested theory.
origin: A consequentialist ethical theory founded by Jeremy Bentham and refined by John Stuart Mill, holding that the right action maximizes overall happiness for the greatest number; the most famous form of consequentialism.
